source.title: Circuit-Diff: Factual Edit-based Intervention Method for Localizing Knowledge in Attribution Graphs

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses neuron polysemanticity as background but studies CLT feature nodes, not neuron poles, neuron explanations, or graphs built from the model's own neurons. Its results therefore do not test any listed claim version.
record.gate_note: The paper's empirical results concern factual edits and CLT attribution-graph features. They do not measure the share or interpretability of neurons, test neuron explanations on held-out activations, or evaluate neuron-based attribution graphs. Related CLT findings are recorded under fits_no_version.
record.test_reason: The study builds a CLT-feature discovery method (Circuit-Diff) on Gemma-2-2B and evaluates CLT graph fidelity and feature-set patching. It never measures neuron monosemanticity shares, InceptionV1 neurons, neuron-based attribution graphs, or neuron-explanation scoring. Neuron polysemanticity and Bills et al. are mentioned only as background citations, so 'cites_only' fits better than 'discusses'. No version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is essentially correct. The authors conclude that editing a fact and re-reading the attribution graph through the same frozen CLT surfaces feature nodes that, on the 24 patched edits, present as knowledge around the object (history, geography, associations), not just its name. They stress limits: frozen-lens degradation, the need for the null floor, small samples, and a weak or absent suppress-side advantage over influence ranking.
record.recipe_differences: A factual-edit-based CLT feature-node discovery method: MEMIT edits Gemma-2-2B, a frozen cross-layer transcoder generates attribution graphs, and node changes are ranked and causally patched. It does not use neuron-pole auditing or neuron explanations.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported outcome changes with the edit-side (inject versus suppress) and with application of the 99th-percentile null floor; the selected nodes' advantage over the graph-influence baseline is stronger on inject than suppress.

fits_no_version.finding: A single MEMIT edit drops frozen-CLT replacement score (median ~0.3) far more than completeness (~0.06) on edited prompts. Neighborhood prompts barely move.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Frozen CLT replacement models lose fidelity locally after weight edits, with error nodes absorbing the gap. This is relevant context for the replacement-model reconstruction-error concern in V5.

fits_no_version.finding: Unfloored edit-diffs flag most of the graph (96.2%/94.4% gained); the null floor reduces this to 14.0%/3.2%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Edit-based CLT feature diffs require null calibration to yield selective candidate sets.

fits_no_version.finding: Group patches of selected CLT feature sets beat count-matched influence rankings on the inject side (9.98 vs 5.90; 8.16 vs 4.94). On the suppress side they are comparable unfloored (−42.4 vs −41.3) and the baseline is ahead under the floor (−35.3 vs −24.8).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Circuit-Diff CLT feature groups are causally effective, but their advantage over influence ranking is side- and calibration-dependent.

record.problems: The paper reports a frozen-lens replacement-score decline after edits; the authors infer that error nodes absorb what the lens cannot model. They note that raw appeared/disappeared readings cover most of the graph, the null-floor percentile was not systematically tuned, and causal evidence rests on group patches over 24 edits (12 for the six-score comparison), which is not enough for a tight effect estimate. They also report substantial overlap with top-influence nodes and limited or absent advantage on the suppress side.
record.rows_left_out: No additional results were left out; empirical results about CLT features are represented where relevant, but none tests a listed neuron-specific version.

untested.parts: All: neuron interpretability shares across models and scale.
All: architecture/tool effects on neuron interpretability.
All: neuron-based attribution graphs without a replacement model. The study uses a CLT replacement and only cites ADAG's MLP-neuron graphs.
All: predictive validity of activating-example explanations. Only cited (Huang et al.).
All: simulation-based scoring of neuron explanations. Only cited (Bills et al.).

record.verdict_notes: Relation changed from 'discusses' to 'cites_only': neuron superposition and Bills et al. appear only in the intro and related-work background. Row r9 has its values swapped: per §5.3, the baseline (−35.3) is ahead of the selected set (−24.8) under the floor. All rows are own-method CLT results and none bears on any version. Neither original source is this study.

versions.untested_parts: Qwen3-32B neuron-pole audit and its one-job, two-job, and not-understood shares.
Neuron interpretability across models, architectures, and scales.
InceptionV1 cat-and-car neuron and recursive generalization versus superposition.
Architecture, regularization, tool quality, and estimates for InceptionV1-sized vision models.
Attribution graphs built from a large model's own neurons; the study uses CLT feature nodes instead.
Whether explanations fitted to activating examples predict other firing locations.
Automated neuron-explanation scoring by simulated activations on new text.
